title: An understanding heart (1 Kings 3:5–9)
hook: offered anything, Solomon asks for "an understanding heart", literally a listening heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, David's last words, sweet singer: one who rules justly is like the light of morning. Your line was like the light of morning. Did you lead fairly in one small way? Today a new book begins, Kings, and a new king is asked a strange question. Day seven hundred fifty-seven.

"Ask what I shall give thee." That's the whole offer. Solomon, David's son, is newly king, and he has gone to Gibeon to bring offerings. That night, the text says, the LORD appears to him in a dream and speaks those words. No limits. No conditions. In the old wish stories, this is where people ask for gold, or for long life, or for their enemies to vanish. Solomon's answer is short and odd. He calls himself a little child who doesn't know how to go out or come in. He has a great people to lead, and he knows he isn't ready. And he asks for one thing. Today's word is what he asked for.
screen: `A DREAM AT GIBEON.` → `ASK WHAT I SHALL GIVE THEE.` → `I AM BUT A LITTLE CHILD.`

segments.voice: The request is in the first book of Kings, chapter three. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, Solomon asks for "an understanding heart to judge Thy people." But the Hebrew is plainer, and stranger. It says lev shomea. Lev is heart. Shomea is hearing. It's the same verb as the word shema in the line from Deuteronomy, Hear, O Israel. So Solomon asks for a hearing heart. A listening heart. Notice what he leaves out. The text lists it itself: God is pleased that he didn't ask for long life, or riches, or the life of his enemies. He asked, God says, for understanding to discern what is just. And the answer comes back larger than the request: the wisdom, and also the riches and honor he never asked for. Why listening, of all things? Solomon's job is to judge, to sit with people's disputes and decide them. A judge can be clever, quick and eloquent, and still never really hear the person standing in front of him. Some readers point out that in the Hebrew Bible the heart isn't only where feelings live; it's also where a person thinks and decides. So a listening heart is a mind that takes in before it rules. And there's a small humility in the request. He doesn't ask to be wise. He asks to be able to hear. In this story, wisdom starts with the ears. It's a request made in a dream, by someone who knew what he didn't know.
screen: `AN UNDERSTANDING HEART.` · `LEV SHOMEA: A HEARING HEART.` · `NOT RICHES, NOT LONG LIFE.` · `WISDOM STARTS WITH THE EARS.` · then, large: `AN UNDERSTANDING HEART TO JUDGE THY PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for wisdom, the listening kind. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one decision or one conversation waiting for you, at work, at home, with someone you love. Before you plan what you'll say, ask what you haven't heard yet. Whose side haven't you listened to all the way through? What might they say if you let them finish? Breathe, and stay with that question. If you pray, you can borrow Solomon's own words and ask for an understanding heart. If you don't, just let your listening widen for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Lev shomea. The Hebrew for a hearing heart, the only thing Solomon asked for when he could have had anything. Today's word.
Your line: a listening heart. Today, in one conversation, let the other person finish completely before you decide anything. Day seven hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Jews read Solomon's dream at Gibeon in the book of Kings, among the Former Prophets; some teachers use the Hebrew phrase lev shomea, a listening heart, as a picture of good judgment.

what it means: he asked for a heart that hears, so he could judge his people fairly.
